120-    """Complete each boundary tab or notch by adding the complementary feature on the opposite side of the foreground object.
121-
122-    Input structure
123-    - The grid has exactly two colors: a dominant background and one foreground object.
124-    - The foreground object is a thick rectilinear shape with one-pixel tabs and notches on its boundary.
125-
126-    Rule
127-    - A foreground tab is a one-neighbor boundary pixel; project through its full row or column span and remove the opposite edge pixel to make a matching notch.
128-    - A background notch is a one-pixel cut with three foreground 4-neighbors; project across the full row or column span and add a tab just outside the opposite edge.
129-    - Notches immediately beside a tab source are not independent sources, because that gap belongs to the tab's local boundary shape.
130-
131-    Key insight
132-    - The changed pixels are not color-specific noise; they are paired jigsaw-like boundary features on opposite sides of the same thick row or column cross-section.
133-    """
134-    g = np.asarray(grid, dtype=int)
135-    bg = get_bg(g)
136-    colors = colors_present(g)
137-    assert len(colors) == 2, "task expects exactly one foreground color and one background"
138-    fg_colors = [color for color in colors if color != bg]
139-    assert len(fg_colors) == 1, "task expects a single foreground color"
140-    fg = fg_colors[0]
141-
142-    mask = g == fg
143-    out = g.copy()
144-
145-    tabs = _tab_sources(mask)
146-    tab_cells = {cell for cell, _direction, _target in tabs}
147-    changes = 0
148-
149-    for _cell, _direction, target in tabs:
150-        if out[target] != bg:
151-            out[target] = bg
152-            changes += 1
153-
154-    for r in range(g.shape[0]):
155-        for c in range(g.shape[1]):
156-            if bool(mask[r, c]):
157-                continue
158-
159-            fg_dirs: list[tuple[int, int]] = []
160-            bg_dirs: list[tuple[int, int]] = []
161-            for dr, dc in DIRS4:
162-                rr, cc = r + dr, c + dc
163-                if in_bounds(mask.shape, rr, cc) and bool(mask[rr, cc]):
164-                    fg_dirs.append((dr, dc))
165-                else:
166-                    bg_dirs.append((dr, dc))
167-
168-            if len(fg_dirs) != 3 or len(bg_dirs) != 1:
169-                continue
170-
171-            outside_dr, outside_dc = bg_dirs[0]
172-            dr, dc = -outside_dr, -outside_dc
173-            side_a = (r - dc, c + dr)
174-            side_b = (r + dc, c - dr)
175-            if side_a in tab_cells or side_b in tab_cells:
176-                continue
177-
178-            target = _outside_opposite_edge(mask, r, c, dr, dc)
179-            if target is not None and not bool(mask[target]):
180-                if out[target] != fg:
181-                    out[target] = fg
182-                    changes += 1

83:def main(grid: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
84-    """
85-    Recover each partially hidden 6x6 ring sprite and stack complete copies from top layer to bottom layer.
86-
87-    Input structure:
88-    - The dominant color is the background.
89-    - Several non-background colors are visible fragments of the same 12-pixel
90-      outline ring in a 6x6 box; small off-template marker pixels are noise.
91-    - Ring fragments overlap, so upper rings replace some expected pixels of
92-      lower rings, and a ring may also be clipped by the input boundary.
93-
94-    Rule:
95-    - Identify every substantial color whose pixels all lie on one translated
96-      copy of the ring template.
97-    - For each missing in-bounds template pixel, the color currently occupying
98-      that pixel is above the hidden ring.
99-    - Topologically sort these occlusion relations from top to bottom, then draw
100-      one complete 6x6 ring for each color in that order on a background canvas.
101-
102-    Key insight:
103-    - The output is not a crop of the scene; it is the layer stack of complete
104-      ring sprites reconstructed from their visible fragments.
105-    """
106-    g = np.asarray(grid, dtype=int)
107-    bg = get_bg(g)
108-    fragments = _find_ring_fragments(g, bg)
109-    order = _layer_order(g, fragments)
110-
111-    out = np.full((_RING_SIZE * len(order), _RING_SIZE), bg, dtype=int)
112-    for i, color in enumerate(order):
113-        base_r = i * _RING_SIZE
114-        for dr, dc in _RING:
115-            out[base_r + dr, dc] = color
116-    return out

70:def main(grid: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
71-    """
72-    Fill rectangles between diagonal marker pairs using a color legend.
73-
74-    Input structure:
75-    - bg grid with a vertical legend at the bottom-left: each row is a (marker_color, fill_color) pair.
76-    - Scattered L-shaped corner markers of each marker color define opposite corners of axis-aligned rectangles.
77-    - Some markers are solid 2×2 blocks instead of corner pairs.
78-
79-    Rule:
80-    - Read legend bottom-to-top; for each entry find all pixels of that marker color.
81-    - Determine which two bbox corners carry L-shaped anchors — the *other* diagonal defines the fill region.
82-    - Fill the diamond (all shortest-path cells between those two corners) with the legend's fill color.
83-    - Solid 2×2 marker blocks are simply recolored to the fill color.
84-    - Later legend entries are protected from earlier fills.
85-
86-    Key insight: The L-shaped anchors sit on the marker diagonal; the fill goes on the opposite diagonal of the bounding box.
87-    """
88-    g = np.asarray(grid, dtype=int)
89-    h, w = g.shape
90-
91-    bg = get_bg(g)
92-    legend_c, entries = _find_legend(g, bg)
93-    assert entries, "legend must contain at least one (marker, fill) entry"
94-
95-    legend_mask = np.zeros_like(g, dtype=bool)
96-    for r, _, _ in entries:
97-        if 0 <= r < h and 0 <= legend_c < w:
98-            legend_mask[r, legend_c] = True
99-        if 0 <= r < h and 0 <= legend_c + 1 < w:
100-            legend_mask[r, legend_c + 1] = True
101-
102-    out = g.copy()
103-
104-    marker_order = [m for _, m, _ in entries]
105-    marker_set = set(marker_order)
106-
107-    # Process legend entries bottom -> top; earlier entries must not destroy later marker pixels.
108-    for i, (_, marker, fill) in enumerate(entries):
109-        eff_fill = int(fill)
110-        marker_pts = set(map(tuple, np.argwhere((g == marker) & (~legend_mask))))
111-        if len(marker_pts) < 2:
112-            continue
113-
114-        rs = [r for r, _ in marker_pts]
115-        cs = [c for _, c in marker_pts]
116-        rmin, rmax = min(rs), max(rs)
117-        cmin, cmax = min(cs), max(cs)
118-
119-        # Protect legend cells and all marker pixels for entries that appear later (higher) in the legend.
120-        future_markers = set(marker_order[i + 1 :])
121-        protect = legend_mask.copy()
122-        for fm in future_markers:
123-            protect |= (g == fm) & (~legend_mask)
124-
125-        # Also protect current marker pixels in the common case (so markers remain visible),
126-        # except when they form a solid 2x2 block (treated as a filled marker that gets recolored).
127-        if rmax - rmin == 1 and cmax - cmin == 1 and len(marker_pts) == 4:
128-            # Solid 2x2 marker: recolor these pixels directly.
129-            block = np.zeros_like(g, dtype=bool)
130-            for r, c in marker_pts:
131-                block[r, c] = True
132-            out[block & (~protect)] = eff_fill
133-            continue
134-        else:
135-            protect |= (g == marker) & (~legend_mask)
136-
137-        if rmin == rmax or cmin == cmax:
138-            continue
139-
140-        tl = (rmin, cmin)
141-        tr = (rmin, cmax)
142-        bl = (rmax, cmin)
143-        br = (rmax, cmax)
144-
145-        tl_anchor = _l_anchor_present(marker_pts, tl[0], tl[1], (0, 1), (1, 0))
146-        tr_anchor = _l_anchor_present(marker_pts, tr[0], tr[1], (0, -1), (1, 0))
147-        bl_anchor = _l_anchor_present(marker_pts, bl[0], bl[1], (0, 1), (-1, 0))
148-        br_anchor = _l_anchor_present(marker_pts, br[0], br[1], (0, -1), (-1, 0))

10-    Stamp translated copies of a monochrome template guided by a singleton pixel layout.

14-    - Singleton pixels elsewhere: exactly one is color T (layout origin); the rest share color O (overlap color).
15-    - Singletons sit on a uniform-spacing lattice.
16-
17-    Rule:
18-    - Convert each singleton's offset from the origin into coarse lattice units.
19-    - Place a template copy at each offset, scaled by template height/width.
20-    - The origin's copy is painted O instead of T.
21-    - Any pixel covered by two or more copies is also recolored to O.
22-
23-    Key insight: The single T-colored singleton identifies both the origin position and the "self" copy, which is uniquely recolored.
24-    """
25-    g = np.array(grid, dtype=int)
26-    bg = int(get_bg(g))
27-    H, W = g.shape

29-    comps = find_components(g, bg=bg, connectivity=4, monochromatic=False, return_format="dict")

42-    singletons: list[tuple[int, int, int]] = []

48-        rr, cc = map(int, comp["coords"][0])
